Story and previous: from IM’s lesson narrative (numbers “purposefully chosen to be difficult” for mental math or double number lines; the focus is finding A% of B “as efficiently as possible”) and Lesson 14’s goals (choose a diagram; the three kinds of problem).
Crux is 15.3, as in Premo’s layer. 15.2 is a fair alternative: it first surfaces the 1% strategy, and IM goal 1 is its goal.

CLO: imGoal is IM goal 2, verbatim, including IM’s $…$ math markup. Function “justify” and mode “out loud” come from it; the unit’s language progression names “justify” for Lessons 15 and 16, so there is no progression note.

Form: “To find ___% of a number, I multiply the number by ___. It works because 1% is the number divided by 100, and ___% is ___ times 1%.” It follows IM’s synthesis argument (divide by 100 for 1%, then multiply by the percentage) and accepts any multiplier a student uses: \(\frac{80}{100}\), 0.8, \(\frac{8}{10}\) or \(\frac{4}{5}\).

Precise terms: “% of,” “1%” and “multiply.” “Percentage” is IM’s productive word for Lesson 15; it is on the board’s language line but not in the precise list, since the exemplar would pass 25 words with it. A reviewer may want it added.
Board lines can’t hold digits, so the language line says “one percent.”

Look-for: IM’s cool-down response multiplies by decimals; it also accepts 1% first, \(\frac{P}{100}\), and 10% steps. IM’s cool-down misconception (Teacher Guide only): ordering by the percentages alone or by the 100% amounts alone.

Per D1: Three Reads to launch, an MLR 8 frame at release, MLR 1 Stronger and Clearer Each Time in the synthesis. MLR 1 is IM’s own routine for 15.3, so IM’s move is kept as written: 2–3 partners in a row, IM’s feedback prompts, a table and an expression in each draft. IM’s synthesis then discusses \(\frac{80}{100} \boldcdot x\) first, with the 1% table.

15.3 is 15 minutes. Card times are estimates: Three Reads about 2 minutes, quiet think time to about 7, partner rounds about 7–11, the class discussion from about 12. Three partner rounds and the expressions discussion may not both fit; the cut keeps two rounds.
15.3 momentIds: m8, m7, m6, in class order (draft, then expressions, then partner rounds). m9 (taking 20% off) is a back-pocket line.
15.2 momentIds: m2 and m3; m3 needs momentCriteria here. m4 (Compare and Connect slipping) is left out: 15.2 isn’t the crux, so its language routine isn’t rehearsed (D7).
NEW (Premo-written, unreviewed): the student drafts on the m8 and synthesis cards; all ifNot questions and goingOn lines; the level frames, stretches and nonverbal ways in.
Non-crux activities carry no language supports (D7).
story: Lesson 15 is near the end of the percentages section. The numbers are too awkward for diagrams, so students find one process for any percentage: multiply by \(\frac{P}{100}\).
previous: In Lesson 14 students chose diagrams to solve all three kinds of percentage problems; today they look for the most efficient way to find a percentage of a number.

clo.imGoal: Generalize a process for finding A% of B and justify (orally) why this can be abstracted as $\frac{A}{100} \boldcdot B$.
clo.form: To find ___% of a number, I multiply the number by ___. It works because 1% is the number divided by 100, and ___% is ___ times 1%.

board.content: We will find a percentage of any number by multiplying, and see why it always works.
board.language: We will justify, out loud, why we multiply to find a “percentage,” using “% of” and “one percent.”

clo.exemplar: To find 80% of a price, I multiply the price by \(\frac{80}{100}\). It works because 1% is the price divided by 100, and 80% is 80 times 1%.
clo.lookFor: The order is 82% of 50 (41), 170% of 30 (51), then 65% of 80 (52). Each value is found by multiplying by a decimal or \(\frac{P}{100}\), by 1% first, or by 10% steps, and the reasoning is shown.

posted.sentence: To find 60% of 45, I multiply 45 by \(\frac{60}{100}\) and get 27. It works because 1% is 45 divided by 100, and 60% is 60 times 1%.

strategies: \(145 \boldcdot \frac{1}{100}\): a bit more than 1, with digits 1, 4, 5, so 1.45.
barriers: Place value past tenths: hundredths in 0.23 and 0.07.
That times \(\frac{1}{100}\) and divide by 100 are the same move.
misconceptions: Writing 7 ÷ 100 as 0.7, one place instead of two.
Multiplying 145 by \(\frac{1}{100}\) as if it made the number bigger.
backPocket: How is multiplying by \(\frac{1}{100}\) related to division?
What is important to remember about dividing a one digit number by 100?
Is your answer more or less than 1? How do you know?
activities.grouping: Whole class: one problem at a time, 30 seconds of quiet think time each, all problems left on display.
activities.monitor: Listen for place-value reasons, not only “move the point.” Pick a couple of students per problem.

strategies: 10% steps: 10% of 250 is 25, so 30% is 75 and 140% is 350.
4% steps: 4% is 10 people, so 44% is 11 of those, 110.
A double number line with a tick every 10%, which gets awkward for 44%.
barriers: 140% is more than the whole, which may still feel odd.
“Attendance at the concert” is the 100% value in every question.
misconceptions: Stopping at 44%: 10% steps reach 40% but not 44%.
Drawing 25 tick marks instead of multiplying 4% and 10 people by 11.
Finding 140% as 40% of 250, leaving out the whole 100%.
backPocket: What smaller percentage could you build 44% from?
Is 140% more or less than the concert crowd?
activities.grouping: Alone, then pairs: quiet think time for all three questions, then each partner explains their reasoning.
activities.monitor: Check in after 2–3 minutes: who has a way to 44%? Note 10% steps, 4% steps and 1% first, to share with 1% last.

m3: Called a less efficient way to 44% first
Asked how the 1% way could work for any percentage

strategies: Multiply each regular price by 0.8: $10 becomes $8.
Find 1% (divide by 100), then multiply by 80: \(\frac{80}{100}\) of the price.
Find 10%, then take 8 of them: for $55, 10% is 5.50 and 8 × 5.50 = 44.
Take 20% off: $55 − $11 = $44, which works but takes two steps.
Expressions that work: \(\frac{80}{100} \boldcdot x\), \(\frac{8}{10} \boldcdot x\), \(\frac{4}{5} \boldcdot x\), \((0.8) \boldcdot x\).
barriers: The letter \(x\) standing for any regular price may be new.
Equivalent fractions: seeing \(\frac{80}{100}\), \(\frac{8}{10}\) and \(\frac{4}{5}\) as one value.
misconceptions: Selecting \(\frac{8}{100} \boldcdot x\) or \((0.08) \boldcdot x\), reading 80% as 8 hundredths.
Selecting \(80 \boldcdot x\) or \(8 \boldcdot x\), using the percent as a plain number.
Language: “You times it by 0.8,” a step with no reason.
backPocket: What percent of the number is \(\frac{8}{100}\) of it?
What is 1% of the regular price? How do you get 80% from it?
Will this expression always work? How do you know?
Does that work for every item? Can you make it one step?
activities.grouping: Alone, then partners in a row: quiet think time for the task, then 2–3 partner rounds revising question 3.
activities.monitor: Check each first draft has a table and an expression. Track who multiplies by 0.8, who goes through 1%, and who uses 10% steps.

threeReads.say: Listen as I read. No numbers yet: what is happening?
threeReads.listenFor: A store is having a sale, and every item costs less than usual.

threeReads.say: Read it again. What does 80% tell us, and 80% of what?
threeReads.listenFor: Each sale price is 80% of that item’s regular price. The regular price is 100%.

threeReads.say: Read it once more. How might we find each sale price?
threeReads.listenFor: Find 10% and take 8 of them, find 1% and take 80, or multiply by a fraction or decimal.

release.successCriteria: In your process sentence, say what you multiply by, and why it works, starting from 1%.
release.say: Say what you multiply by. Then say why, starting from 1%.
talkMoments: In the partner rounds, each student reads their process sentence with Today’s frame.
The listener asks one question: “Will this expression always work? How do you know?”

emerging.frame: I multiply by ___. Because 1% is the number ÷ 100, ___% is ___ times 1%.
emerging.stretch: They try their process on one more price, such as $10, and say the sale price.
emerging.nonverbal: On a percentage table (100, 1, 80), they draw the ÷ 100 arrow, then the × 80 arrow.

developing.frame: To find ___% of a number, I multiply by ___. It works because 1% is the number ÷ 100, and ___% is ___ times 1%.
developing.stretch: They name one other expression that also works, and say why it is equal.
developing.nonverbal: They circle every expression that matches their process and cross out one that doesn’t.

expanding.frame: To find ___% of a number, I multiply the number by ___. It works because 1% is the number divided by 100, and ___% is ___ times 1%.
expanding.stretch: They explain why \(\frac{8}{10}\) times the price gives the same sale price.
expanding.nonverbal: They write their process as one expression under their table and point to where each part comes from.

synthesis.routine: MLR1: Stronger and Clearer Each Time
steps: Check each first draft of question 3 has a table and an expression.
Students meet 2–3 partners in a row. Each reads their process; the listener asks “Can you explain how…” or “Will this expression always work?”
After each partner, writers revise, borrowing ideas and words.
As a class, discuss \(\frac{80}{100} \boldcdot x\) first, with the table 100 | \(x\), 1, 80. Ask students where each row shows up in their final drafts.
Then partners decide which other expressions equal \(\frac{80}{100} \boldcdot x\), and why.
synthesis.prompt: Where does each row of the table show up in the final draft?
synthesis.sounds: The 100 row is the regular price. The 1 row is the price divided by 100, for 1%. The 80 row is 80 of those, \(\frac{80}{100}\) times the price.

rehearsal.name: Do the warm-up yourself
rehearsal.where: Before class. Solve the number talk: four expressions, found mentally.
rehearsal.ask: Find each value in your head. How is multiplying by \(\frac{1}{100}\) like dividing by 100?
rehearsal.aim: Know all four values and a place-value reason for each.
notes: 50 is half of 100, so the answer is one half.
145 is a bit more than 100, so the answer is a bit more than 1.
checks: Gave a place-value reason for at least one
Linked times \(\frac{1}{100}\) to dividing by 100

rehearsal.name: A student divides 7 by 100
rehearsal.where: About 4 minutes into Activity 15.1. The fourth problem is up, with the first three still displayed.
rehearsal.ask: What do you say to the class?
rehearsal.aim: Students explain how far 7 moves when divided by 100.
say: What is important to remember about dividing a one digit number by 100?
checks: Asked the class, not just the student, what to remember
Linked it to the problem before, 50 ÷ 100
Didn’t give the rule yourself
rehearsal.goingOn: They know dividing by 100 makes 7 smaller. They moved one place, not two.

rehearsal.name: Do the audience task yourself
rehearsal.where: Before class. Solve the task: 250 people came to the concert.
show: Attendance at a basketball game was 30% of attendance at the concert.
Attendance at the drama play was 140% of attendance at the concert.
Attendance at literacy night was 44% of attendance at the concert.
rehearsal.ask: How many people came to each activity? Find 44% two different ways.
rehearsal.aim: Know all three counts, and two ways to reach 44%.
notes: 10% steps: 10% of 250 is 25. Multiply for 30% and 140%.
4% steps: 4% is 10 people. 44% is 11 of those.
1% first: divide 250 by 100, then multiply by 44. IM shares this last.
checks: Got 75, 350 and 110 people
Found 44% with 4% or 1% steps, not 10% steps alone
Kept 250 people at 100% for all three

rehearsal.name: A student is stuck at 44%
rehearsal.where: About 4 minutes into Activity 15.2. Students are in quiet think time. You check in, as IM suggests.
show: Question 3: Attendance at literacy night was 44% of attendance at the concert.
rehearsal.student: A student stops and says: “44 isn’t a ten.”
rehearsal.ask: What do you say to this student?
rehearsal.aim: The student builds 44% from a smaller percentage they choose.
say: What smaller percentage could you build 44% from?
checks: Started from the 40% they already had
Asked for a smaller step without naming one
Didn’t tell them to find 1%
rehearsal.goingOn: They used 10% steps well and reached 40%. The last 4% needs a smaller step.
rehearsal.ifNot: You have 40%. How much more do you need?

rehearsal.name: Choose who shares first
rehearsal.where: About 10 minutes into Activity 15.2. You heard the first two answers briefly. Now the class discusses literacy night.
show: Pair A · double number line with 25 tick marks, one every 4%.
Pair B · “4% is 10 people, so 11 of those.”
rehearsal.ask: Who do you call first, and who last?
rehearsal.aim: Pairs share so the 1% way comes last.
say: Start us off. How did you find 44% of 250?
checks: Called a less efficient way to 44% first
Saved the 1% way for last
Asked how the 1% way could work for any percentage
rehearsal.why: IM: save the 1% strategy for last. It works for every percentage, much as finding a unit rate solves any ratio problem.

rehearsal.name: Do the sale task yourself
rehearsal.where: Before class. Solve the task students do today: every item is 80% of its regular price.
show: During a sale, every item in a store is 80% of its regular price.
Select all of the expressions that could be used to find 80% of \(x\).
rehearsal.ask: Find each sale price. Write the process you repeated. Which expressions find 80% of \(x\)?
rehearsal.aim: Know every sale price, a process, and which expressions work.
notes: Multiply each regular price by 0.8, or by \(\frac{80}{100}\).
Find 1% by dividing by 100, then take 80 of it.
Find 10%, then take 8 of it; or take 20% off.
IM’s synthesis starts the expressions with \(\frac{80}{100} \boldcdot x\).
checks: Got $8 for the T-shirt and $0.80, $3.20, $8, $44, $96 in the table
Described one process for every price: multiply by 0.8 or \(\frac{80}{100}\)

rehearsal.name: Read the task three times
rehearsal.where: Start of Activity 15.3. The task is up, with the price table and expressions covered.
show: During a sale, every item in a store is 80% of its regular price.
If the regular price of a T-shirt is $10, what is its sale price?
rehearsal.ask: Read the first part aloud three times. After each read, ask one question. Nobody solves yet.
rehearsal.aim: Students know the regular price is the whole before anyone solves.

rounds.ask: You’ve read it once. What do you ask?
rounds.aim: Students say what is happening, with no numbers.

rounds.ask: You’ve read it twice. What do you ask?
rounds.aim: Students say what 80% is a percentage of.

rounds.ask: You’ve read it three times. What do you ask?
rounds.aim: Students suggest ways to find a sale price, without solving.

checks: Read 1: asked what is happening, with no numbers
Read 2: asked what 80% tells us, and 80% of what
Read 3: asked how we might find each sale price, and took ideas without solving
rehearsal.why: IM: Three Reads makes sure students know what they’re being asked to do. Here, it fixes the regular price as 100% before any price is worked.
runIt: Read 1: read the first part aloud. Ask what is happening, with no numbers.
Read 2: read it again. Ask what 80% tells us, and 80% of what.
Read 3: read it once more. Ask how we might find a sale price. Take ideas; nobody solves.
Then uncover the price table and expressions, and start quiet think time.

rehearsal.name: Send students to work
rehearsal.where: About 2 minutes into Activity 15.3. Three Reads just ended. Next: quiet think time, then partner rounds on question 3.
rehearsal.ask: What must every process sentence include? What do you tell the class?
rehearsal.aim: Students know their sentence needs what they multiply by, and why.
say: Say what you multiply by. Then say why, starting from 1%.
notes: Success criteria: In your process sentence, say what you multiply by, and why it works, starting from 1%.
When partners talk: in the partner rounds, each student reads their process sentence with Today’s frame.
Then: the listener asks one question: “Will this expression always work? How do you know?”
checks: Named what every sentence needs: the multiplier and the reason from 1%
Pointed to Today’s frame on the board
Told them they’ll read it to 2–3 partners
rehearsal.sounds: To find 80% of a price, I multiply the price by \(\frac{80}{100}\). It works because 1% is the price divided by 100, and 80% is 80 times 1%.
rehearsal.why: Goal 2 asks students to justify the process, not only state it. Naming the reason now means every draft has one to sharpen.

rehearsal.name: Help a student say why
rehearsal.where: About 5 minutes into Activity 15.3. Students are drafting question 3 in quiet think time.
show: Their draft for question 3: “You times it by 0.8.”
rehearsal.student: A student’s first draft reads: “You times it by 0.8.”
rehearsal.ask: What do you say to this student?
rehearsal.aim: The student says why multiplying by 0.8 gives 80%, starting from 1%.
checks: Asked every level the same question: why does times 0.8 give 80%
Gave their level’s frame or nonverbal way in
Didn’t write the reason for them
rehearsal.sounds: To find 80% of a price, I multiply the price by 0.8. It works because 1% is the price divided by 100, and 80% is 80 times 1%.
rehearsal.goingOn: They found the step they repeated for every price. Why 0.8 gives 80%, the justify part, isn’t in words yet.

rehearsal.name: A student picks 8 hundredths
rehearsal.where: About 7 minutes into Activity 15.3. Students are on the expressions question.
show: Their table, above: regular price $10, sale price $8.
rehearsal.student: A student has selected \(\frac{8}{100} \boldcdot x\) and \((0.08) \boldcdot x\) for 80% of \(x\).
rehearsal.ask: What do you say to this student?
rehearsal.aim: The student tests the expressions on a price they know and revises.
say: What percent of the number is \(\frac{8}{100}\) of it?
checks: Asked them to name the percent the expression finds
Pointed them to a price they already worked, such as $10
Didn’t cross out the expressions for them
rehearsal.goingOn: They know a percent becomes a fraction over 100. They read 80% as 8 hundredths, mixing tenths and hundredths.
rehearsal.ifNot: Try \(\frac{8}{100}\) on the $10 T-shirt. Do you get the sale price?

rehearsal.name: Get partners asking questions
rehearsal.where: About 9 minutes into Activity 15.3. Partner rounds have started. Pairs are reading drafts to each other.
show: One pair: each reads a draft, both nod, and they stand to find new partners.
rehearsal.ask: What do you say to this pair before they move on?
rehearsal.aim: The listener asks a question, and the writer changes one thing.
say: Will this expression always work? How do you know?
checks: Gave the listener a question to ask
Waited for the writer to change one thing
Didn’t let pairs swap drafts without a question
rehearsal.why: IM: feedback prompts help students strengthen their ideas and clarify their language. Without a question, the next draft is the same as the last.

rehearsal.routine: MLR1: Stronger and Clearer Each Time
rehearsal.name: Make the reason stronger
rehearsal.where: About 12 minutes into Activity 15.3. Partner rounds are done. One student’s first and final drafts are up.
show: Final draft: “I multiply the price by 0.8. 1% is the price divided by 100, so 80% is 80 of those.”
rehearsal.ask: Both drafts are up. What do you ask the class?
rehearsal.aim: Students tie each table row to a part of the final draft.
notes: Point to the table, then the final draft. Let students make the match:
say: Where does each row of the table show up in the final draft?
checks: Had every student revise after at least two partners
Started the class discussion with \(\frac{80}{100} \boldcdot x\) and the 1% row
Let students match the rows to the draft
rehearsal.sounds: The 100 row is the regular price. The 1 row is the price divided by 100, for 1%. The 80 row is 80 of those, \(\frac{80}{100}\) times the price.
rehearsal.why: IM: Stronger and Clearer gives students a structured chance to revise and refine their own strategies. Here, the reason from 1% is what gets clearer.
runIt: Check each first draft of question 3 has a table and an expression.
Students meet 2–3 partners in a row. The listener asks “Can you explain how…” or “Will this expression always work?”
After each partner, writers revise, borrowing ideas and words.
As a class, discuss \(\frac{80}{100} \boldcdot x\) first, with the 1% table. Ask where each row shows up in a final draft.
Then partners decide which other expressions are equal, and why.

ideas: To find \(P\%\) of a number, multiply the number by \(\frac{P}{100}\).
It works because 1% of the number is the number divided by 100, and \(P\%\) is \(P\) times that.
So 80% of $55 is \(\frac{80}{100}\) times 55, or 0.8 times 55: $44.
lessonSynthesis.pointTo: Point to the 15.3 table (100, 1, 80) and a final draft beside it. If you taught 15.2, point to its 1% row too: 2.5 people.

check.question: How could you find 32% of 500? Say it with Today’s frame.
check.sounds: To find 32% of 500, I multiply 500 by \(\frac{32}{100}\). It works because 1% is 500 divided by 100, and 32% is 32 times 1%.

beforeClass: For Three Reads in 15.3: display the task with the price table and expressions covered until after the third read.
For the release: have the frames for your students’ levels ready to post or hand out.
For Stronger and Clearer (MLR 1): post the prompts “Can you explain how…” and “Will this expression always work? How do you know?”
For the discussion: draw IM’s table, percentage | regular price, rows 100, 1, 80, ready to fill. Have calculators available.

cuts.note: Keep to IM’s 5 minutes: a couple of students per problem, then IM’s two questions.
Hear the first two answers briefly; spend the discussion on 44% of 250, with the 1% way last.
If time is short, do two partner rounds, not three. Never cut the revising, or the discussion of \(\frac{80}{100} \boldcdot x\) from the 1% row.
